title: When I kept silent (Psalm 32)
hook: holding a wrong in, my bones wasted away; confessing, I was forgiven

segments.voice: Yesterday, Psalm thirty: yalin, weeping stays the night like a guest, and your line, joy comes in the morning.

A sharp word to a friend, three weeks back. Credit taken for something that wasn't quite yours. A small lie, then another to cover it. Nobody found out. And yet it sits there, at night, in the shoulders, in the stomach. Something that small, held in, can get heavy. Long ago, someone wrote that weight down in a psalm that reads almost like a medical chart of a guilty conscience.
screen: `SOMETHING SMALL, NEVER SAID.` → `IT SITS IN THE SHOULDERS.` → `A CHART OF A GUILTY CONSCIENCE.`

segments.voice: Psalm thirty-two starts at the end of the story, with relief, in the King James Bible: "Blessed is he whose transgression is forgiven, whose sin is covered." Then it goes back to tell how it got there. "When I kept silence, my bones waxed old through my roaring all the day long. For day and night thy hand was heavy upon me: my moisture is turned into the drought of summer." Bones aging. Groaning all day. Dried out, like a field in August. The silence wasn't peaceful. It was exhausting. Then the turn, and it comes fast: "I acknowledged my sin unto thee, and mine iniquity have I not hid. I said, I will confess my transgressions unto the LORD; and thou forgavest the iniquity of my sin." I said I will confess, and you forgave. A weight carried for who knows how long lifts in a single breath. Then God speaks: "I will instruct thee and teach thee in the way which thou shalt go: I will guide thee with mine eye." And a gentle warning: don't be like a horse or a mule that has to be steered with a bit and bridle. Paul quotes its opening in his letter to the Romans. Western Christian tradition groups it with the penitential psalms, the psalms of turning back. Augustine's biographer says that as he was dying, Augustine had the penitential psalms copied and put on the wall where he could read them from his bed. Christians practice confession differently. Catholics and Orthodox Christians confess to a priest in a sacrament. Some Protestants confess directly to God, some in a prayer said together in church, and some to a trusted friend, as the letter of James puts it: confess your faults one to another.
screen: `IT STARTS WITH RELIEF.` · `SILENCE DRIED ME OUT.` · `I SAID I WILL, AND THOU FORGAVEST.` · `NOT LIKE A HORSE OR A MULE.` · then, large: `WHEN I KEPT SILENCE, MY BONES WAXED OLD.`

segments.voice: Let one small wrong you've been carrying in silence come to mind, not the biggest one, and notice where it sits in your body. Then say it plainly: if you pray, to God, in your own words; if you don't, out loud to the empty room, or on a piece of paper. Then notice your shoulders.
Penitential psalms. The group of psalms, including this one, that the church prays when turning back to God after sin.
Your line: silence was heavy. One honest sentence, and it lifted. Day four hundred nineteen, done.

howItsDone: Catholic and Orthodox Christians confess in the sacrament of reconciliation; some Protestants confess privately to God or in prayers of confession in worship. Psalm 32 is one of the penitential psalms, prayed in Lent in some churches.

chat.says: Why does that psalm say keeping quiet about a wrong made things worse?
options: Holding it in dried him out like summer drought; he confessed, and he was forgiven.
Someone found out his secret, and the shame of being caught wore him down.
It says the real peace comes from forgetting the wrong and simply moving on.
chat.meaning: In Psalm 32, silence wore him out like summer drought. When he said I will confess, he was forgiven in a single breath.

transgression.meaning: an old word for a wrong, a line crossed

notes: Editor review (y2 days 407–424): hook no longer tells the listener what they did and feel ("You said something sharp... You feel it"); cut "Christians have treasured this psalm"; "the church counts it among the seven" became Western tradition grouping it with the penitential psalms (the number isn't in the cited text; also removed from howItsDone and trapdoor); "many Protestants" softened, James 5:16 now voiced, and the sweeping "All of them know the weight of the silence" cut.

Possidius, Vita Augustini 31: Augustine had the penitential psalms of David (Possidius says 'very few', often read as four) copied and placed on the wall by his bed. The script avoids the number. Confirm.
The seven penitential psalms (6, 32, 38, 51, 102, 130, 143) as a grouping dates to Cassiodorus (sixth century); the script no longer states the number. Confirm.
The heading reads 'A Psalm of David'; the script says 'long ago' without dating it.
